blocks.text: Every system that does real work eventually fails at something, a network hiccup, invalid input, a downstream service being down. MCP handles this with a single, consistent error shape used everywhere, so a client never has to guess what a failure looks like depending on which method or server produced it.
1. The Standard Error Shape

blocks.alt: code, message, and data make up an error

blocks.text: An error response carries an error object with, at minimum, a code identifying the type of failure and a message describing it in human-readable terms, an optional data field can carry extra structured detail specific to that error.

blocks.title: A quick way to remember it
blocks.content: code for machines, message for humans, data for anything extra a specific error needs to carry.

blocks.text: This shape is identical whether the failure came from a tools/call, a resources/read, or any other method, a client only ever needs one piece of error-handling logic for the whole protocol.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A missing error field alongside a missing result field would leave a client with no idea what happened at all, the protocol requires one or the other always be present.

blocks.text: 2. code vs message: Two Different Audiences

blocks.alt: code is machine-readable while message is human-readable

blocks.text: The code is meant for a program to check and branch on, stable and machine-readable, the message is meant for a human to read, more descriptive and potentially changing wording over time, a client should generally branch on code, not on parsing the message text.
A message can be improved or reworded over time without breaking anything, since well-written client code never depends on its exact text, only on the stable code field.
This split mirrors the general principle behind stable identifiers versus human-facing labels found throughout well-designed software interfaces.
3. Common Error Categories

blocks.alt: Parse error, invalid params, and method not found are common error categories

blocks.text: Most MCP servers group their errors into a handful of recurring categories, invalid input, missing permissions, resource not found, and internal failure, having a consistent, small set of categories makes error handling logic reusable across many different tools.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Category","Example code","Typical cause"],"rows":[["Invalid input","invalid_arguments","Missing or malformed parameter"],["Not found","not_found","Requested resource does not exist"],["Permission","unauthorized","Caller lacks required access"],["Internal","internal_error","Unexpected failure inside the server"]]}

code.content:
# a lookup used to decide default handling per category
CATEGORY_BY_CODE = {"invalid_arguments": "input", "not_found": "lookup", "unauthorized": "permission", "internal_error": "server"}

blocks.text: Some servers add a fifth category for rate limiting specifically, distinct from a plain internal error, since the correct client reaction, waiting and retrying later, is quite different.
4. The Optional data Field

The data field lets a server attach extra, structured detail beyond a plain message, which field failed validation, what the valid range was, this extra detail can let a sophisticated client offer a more specific, helpful response than the raw message text alone would allow.
A client that does not need this extra detail can simply ignore the data field entirely, its presence never breaks a client that only checks code and message.
Keep the data field itself simple and predictable in shape per error code, a client relying on it should be able to trust its structure will not change unexpectedly.
5. Designing Error Codes for Your Own Server

A good error code is short, stable, and specific enough to be actionable, invalid_arguments is useful, error is not, since a client cannot meaningfully branch on something that vague, picking a small, well-documented set of codes upfront pays off as a server grows.
Documenting the full list of error codes a server can return, alongside its tool descriptions, gives client authors a complete picture of what to prepare for.
Reusing well-known, widely recognized codes like not_found and unauthorized where they genuinely apply also helps a developer new to your server feel immediately at home.
6. How a Client Should React to Different Errors

blocks.alt: An error code determines a different client reaction

blocks.text: Not every error deserves the same response, an invalid_arguments error usually means the caller, often the model, should reconsider and retry with corrected input, an internal_error might warrant a retry after a short delay, an unauthorized error should not be retried at all without first fixing the underlying permission issue.

blocks.title: A useful default
blocks.content: When in doubt about a specific error code, treating it as non-retryable and surfacing it clearly is safer than guessing it is safe to retry automatically.

blocks.text: Building this reaction logic once, as a small, shared function, keeps every tool call in a codebase handling errors the same consistent way.

code.content:
# a small shared reaction table used across a whole application
REACTIONS = {"invalid_arguments": "fix_and_retry", "internal_error": "retry_with_backoff", "unauthorized": "escalate"}

blocks.text: 7. Errors Should Never Leak Sensitive Details

An error message revealing internal file paths, stack traces, or credentials is a real security risk, a well-designed server returns enough detail to be useful without exposing internals that an attacker, or an overly curious model, should never see.
A good habit is reviewing every error message a server can produce and asking, would I be comfortable with an untrusted caller reading this exact text.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Detail","Safe to include","Risky to include"],"rows":[["Which field was invalid","Yes",""],["Internal file path","","No"],["Database error text","","No"]]}

blocks.text: This same review discipline is worth applying whenever a new tool is added to a server, checking its full set of possible error messages before it ever ships to a real caller.
8. Distinguishing Protocol Errors From Tool Errors

blocks.alt: A protocol error is compared against a tool execution error

blocks.text: A protocol-level error means something went wrong with the MCP exchange itself, an unknown method, a malformed request, a tool-level error means the tool ran but the underlying operation failed, like a file not being found, both use the same error shape but represent different layers of failure.

A protocol-level error usually indicates a bug or mismatch in the client or server implementation itself, a tool-level error usually reflects a normal, expected real-world condition like a missing file.

blocks.title: A quick test
blocks.content: If the exact same call would have succeeded with slightly different arguments, it is almost certainly a tool-level error, not a protocol-level one.

blocks.text: A well-written server test suite typically covers both layers separately, one set of tests exercising malformed protocol messages, another exercising valid protocol messages with invalid underlying tool arguments.
9. Errors and Retries: Idempotency Matters

blocks.alt: A failed call is checked for whether it is safe to retry

blocks.text: Whether an error is safe to retry automatically depends heavily on whether the underlying operation is idempotent, covered in the Tools lesson earlier in this curriculum, retrying a failed read is almost always safe, retrying a failed payment is not, without additional safeguards.

blocks.title: A useful default policy
blocks.content: When uncertain whether an operation is idempotent, treat it as non-idempotent and avoid automatic retries, a missed retry is usually less costly than an accidental duplicate action.

blocks.text: 10. Logging Errors for Later Debugging

Every error response is worth logging on the server side, including its code, message, and the request that triggered it, this log becomes the primary trail for diagnosing why a specific call failed after the fact.
Structured logs, with code and relevant request details as separate searchable fields rather than one long string, make it far easier to spot patterns across many failures.
Correlating a logged error with the specific session and request id that produced it makes tracing a bug back to its root cause dramatically faster.

Retaining error logs for a reasonable period, rather than discarding them immediately, also supports spotting slower, less obvious patterns like a specific error code gradually increasing in frequency over weeks.
11. Errors Surfaced to the Model vs the End User

blocks.alt: A model-facing error is compared against a user-facing error

blocks.text: A raw error code like invalid_arguments is perfectly fine context for a model to reason about and recover from, but a human user usually needs a friendlier, translated explanation, the host application is typically responsible for this translation.
A model reasoning about an invalid_arguments error can often correct its own mistake and retry immediately, without ever needing a human to intervene.
12. Testing Error Paths, Not Just Success Paths

A server test suite that only ever tests the happy path misses an entire category of bugs, deliberately calling a tool with missing or invalid arguments and checking the exact error shape returned is just as important as testing successful calls.
Some teams maintain a dedicated suite of negative test cases, one per known error code, run alongside their normal positive tests on every change to the server.
13. Versioning Error Codes Over Time

Adding a new, more specific error code alongside existing ones is usually safe, removing or renaming an existing code can break any client logic that checks for it specifically, treat published error codes with the same care as any other part of a server public interface.

A changelog documenting when a specific error code was introduced, or when its meaning changed, is a small investment that pays off enormously for anyone maintaining a client against that server long term.

This is exactly the same discipline applied to prompt versioning and resource versioning covered elsewhere in this curriculum, a public interface, once published, deserves careful, deliberate evolution.
14. A Worked Example
Trace a tool call that fails validation, and how the client reacts to the resulting error.

code.content:
result = client.call_tool("get_weather", {})   # missing required city argument
if "error" in result:
    print(result["error"]["code"], "-", result["error"]["message"])
    # invalid_arguments - city is required

blocks.text: Notice the client never needed to parse the message text to decide what happened, checking the code field alone was enough to branch correctly.
If the same call were retried with the corrected city argument, the exact same request shape would now succeed and return a normal result instead.
15. Common Mistakes When Designing Error Responses

items: Using a single generic error code for every possible failure, giving a client nothing useful to branch on.
Putting sensitive internal details, like file paths or stack traces, directly into the message field.
Automatically retrying every error the same way, without considering whether the underlying operation is safe to repeat.
Forgetting to log errors on the server side, losing the ability to diagnose a failure after the fact.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is changing the meaning of an existing error code over time without renaming it, silently breaking any client logic that depended on its old, specific meaning.
An eighth common mistake is treating every error as equally severe in logs, drowning out genuinely critical failures among a flood of routine, expected validation errors.
16. Practice: Design an Error Taxonomy

For a small task-management MCP server, sketch out a short list of error codes it might need, covering invalid input, missing tasks, and permission issues, and write one example error object for each.

code.content:
errors = [
    {"code": "invalid_arguments", "message": "title is required"},
    {"code": "task_not_found", "message": "No task with that id exists"},
    {"code": "unauthorized", "message": "You do not have access to this task"},
]

blocks.text: Once sketched, consider which of these three error types would be safe to retry automatically, and which should always be surfaced to a human or the model without a silent retry.
As a final step, write the exact client-side reaction each error code should trigger, retry, surface to the user, or escalate, mirroring the reaction table pattern covered earlier in this lesson.
Key Takeaway

Every MCP error response shares the same shape, a stable code for programs to branch on, a readable message for humans, and optional structured data for extra detail, using this shape consistently, and reacting to different error categories appropriately, is what lets a client recover gracefully instead of failing unpredictably.

This lesson builds on the Responses lesson from the MCP Fundamentals module, and connects forward to Batching next, which looks at how multiple requests, and their potential errors, can be sent and received together.

The testing-error-paths habit from the newly added section is one of the highest-value, lowest-effort improvements a server author can make, deliberately exercising failure cases catches real bugs long before a user ever encounters them.
